column1: boundaries|How should a service boundary be chosen instead of creating one service per database table?|Use business capability, ownership, consistency needs, and operational independence as inputs. Keep highly coupled invariants together where possible. Separate deployment adds network failure, versioning, observability, and coordination costs; start with a modular monolith when that is the simpler justified choice.|business~capability;consisten~invariant;network~operational;trade~cost|Every table should automatically become a microservice.|Orders and payment status must coordinate across services. Propose boundaries and explain failure handling.|Keep each service's owned state explicit, define idempotent contracts, and coordinate through durable events or a saga where appropriate. Do not claim an ordinary local database transaction spans independent services.|outbox,aws-idempotency|service

contracts|What should an evolvable API or event contract specify?|Define request and response schemas, version compatibility, error semantics, authentication/authorization, idempotency, ordering assumptions, and timeout/retry policy. Add compatible fields before requiring them and test consumers; a schema alone does not describe delivery semantics.|schema;compatib~version;error;idempot~ordering|Changing an event field type is automatically backward compatible.|A producer changes an optional numeric field into a required string and old consumers fail. Design a safer migration.|Add a compatible representation, support both during rollout, validate consumer compatibility, then retire the old field deliberately. Test replay of older stored events as well as live traffic.|schema,kafka|compatibility

rate-limit|How do token-bucket and fixed-window rate limiters differ?|A token bucket replenishes a bounded token supply, allowing a controlled burst while bounding average rate. Fixed windows count requests per interval and can allow boundary bursts. Distributed enforcement requires atomic state updates, tenant/key scope, and an explicit fail-open or fail-closed policy.|token~bucket;burst;atomic~distributed;window|A fixed window prevents all traffic bursts at interval boundaries.|An API permits 100 requests per minute but users send 200 around a minute boundary. Explain and redesign it.|Two adjacent fixed windows can permit that pattern. Use a token bucket or sliding-window policy suited to the service, atomically enforce scoped state, and return useful retry information.|aws-ratelimit|token

backoff|Why should retries have deadlines, jitter, and a shared attempt budget?|Exponential delay reduces immediate repeated load, jitter spreads synchronized clients, and a deadline bounds total user-visible time. Layered retries can multiply attempts; assign one responsible layer or coordinate a budget. Only retry operations whose semantics allow it.|jitter;deadline~budget;layer~multiply;idempot~semantics|Adding retries independently at every layer cannot amplify load.|A request passes through three services, each making three attempts. How can retry amplification be reduced?|Potential downstream attempts multiply. Bound retries at a chosen layer, propagate deadlines, use jitter, and ensure idempotent operations before replaying side effects.|aws-retry|jitter

breaker|How should half-open circuit-breaker probes be limited?|After an open cooldown, admit a bounded number of probes rather than all waiting callers. Close only after a defined recovery signal, otherwise reopen. Tune error thresholds and time windows to traffic and dependency semantics; a breaker is not a substitute for timeout limits.|half-open~probe;bounded~limit;reopen~close;timeout|Half-open means every caller may immediately retry.|A dependency recovers briefly then collapses when the breaker half-opens. Explain the likely herd and mitigation.|Too many concurrent probes can recreate overload. Limit probe concurrency, use a cooldown and explicit success criteria, and retain per-request timeouts and retry budgets.|aws-retry|overload

consumer-groups|How do Kafka consumer groups, partitions, and offsets relate?|Within a consumer group a partition is assigned to at most one active consumer at a time. Multiple groups can independently consume the same topic. Offsets track progress per group and partition; ordering is partition-local, not a global topic order.|partition;group;offset;ordering~order|Kafka guarantees one global order across all partitions.|A topic has four partitions and one group has ten consumers. How many can actively own partitions, ignoring rebalances?|At most four consumers in that group own partitions simultaneously. Extra consumers can be idle; another group has its own independent assignments and offsets.|kafka|consumer group

at-least-once|Why can an at-least-once consumer execute a side effect twice?|If a side effect commits before its offset/acknowledgment and the consumer crashes, redelivery can repeat it. Use idempotent side effects or atomic deduplication with the state mutation. A broker's exactly-once mechanism does not automatically cover arbitrary external APIs.|crash~redeliver;offset~ack;idempot~dedup;external|At-least-once delivery guarantees each side effect occurs exactly once.|A consumer sends an email then crashes before committing its offset. What behavior follows and how can it be controlled?|The message may be delivered again and another email sent. Persist an idempotent send record or use a provider idempotency contract and reconcile ambiguous outcomes.|kafka,aws-idempotency|at-least-once

outbox|How does a transactional outbox address the database-and-message dual-write problem?|Write the business state and an outbox row in one local transaction. A relay publishes committed outbox records and retries failures. Relay publication can be duplicated, so consumers still need idempotency; the pattern does not make every external action exactly once.|transaction;outbox;relay;idempot~duplicate|The outbox pattern eliminates all duplicate deliveries.|A database commit succeeds but the service crashes before publishing its event. Repair the architecture.|Persist the event with the state change in the same transaction and let a recoverable relay publish it. Monitor lag and deduplicate downstream processing.|outbox|transaction

isolation|Why does database isolation level matter for check-then-write invariants?|Concurrent transactions can observe snapshots and interleave differently at each isolation level. Enforce invariants through unique/check constraints, row locks, atomic updates, or serializable transactions with retries as appropriate. Serializable isolation can abort conflicting transactions rather than magically making every commit succeed.|isolation;constraint~lock~atomic;serializ;retry~abort|Serializable transactions never need retry handling.|Two transactions both observe one remaining seat and sell it. Give a safe database approach.|Use an atomic conditional update or lock the seat/inventory row and check within the transaction; alternatively use an invariant-preserving serializable design and retry serialization failures.|postgres|serialization

rls|What guarantees and exceptions must be considered for PostgreSQL row-level security?|RLS policies filter or check row access when enabled, with default deny when no applicable policy exists. Superusers and BYPASSRLS roles bypass policies; table owners normally bypass unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is used. Trusted tenant context, role permissions, and connection-pool reset remain necessary.|policy;BYPASSRLS~superuser;owner~FORCE;tenant~context|RLS automatically restricts every superuser and table owner.|A pooled service runs queries as the table owner and relies on RLS for tenant isolation. What can go wrong?|The owner may bypass RLS. Use an appropriate restricted role or FORCE policy where appropriate, establish trusted tenant context transactionally, and test pool reuse across tenants.|postgres-rls|BYPASSRLS

cache|How can a TTL cache avoid serving a stale asynchronous refresh after invalidation?|Treat authoritative storage as the source of truth, scope keys by entity and tenant/version, and invalidate or version entries on updates. A refresh should compare its captured version before publishing. TTL bounds age but alone does not order competing refreshes or guarantee freshness.|authoritat~source;version;invalidate;TTL~stale|A TTL alone guarantees every read is the newest value.|A slow cache refresh starts, a write invalidates the entry, then the old refresh completes. How do you prevent stale repopulation?|Associate refreshes with a generation/version and reject a result from an older generation. Combine this with bounded refresh work and a documented stale-serving policy.|aws-idempotency,postgres|version

observability|How do logs, metrics, and traces complement one another in a distributed request?|Metrics reveal rates, latency, saturation, and error trends; traces show causal request paths and dependency spans; structured logs provide discrete event details. Correlate using trace/request identifiers while protecting secrets and avoiding unbounded metric-label cardinality.|metric;trace;log;cardinal~secret|Logging every request body is always the safest observability strategy.|A latency spike occurs only for one dependency path. What signals help isolate it without leaking tokens?|Use latency/error metrics to locate the interval, sampled distributed traces to identify slow spans, and correlated redacted logs for details. Do not put tokens or per-user IDs in unbounded metric labels.|otel,sre-monitor|traces

recovery|What must a recovery plan specify beyond having backups?|Define recovery point and time objectives, consistent restore procedures, verification, access control, and replay/idempotency behavior. Test restores under failure conditions. A backup that exists but has never been restored is not evidence that recovery meets the objectives.|RPO~point;RTO~time;restore;test~verify|Having a backup file proves recovery time objectives are met.|A restored database is an hour behind the event broker. How should restart and replay be planned?|Choose a consistent recovery boundary, reconcile offsets/state, replay idempotently, and validate invariants. Document tolerated data loss and expected recovery time before restoring production traffic.|sre-testing,kafka|recovery

ordering|How should a Kafka application preserve per-entity ordering while scaling?|Choose a key that routes an entity's events to one partition, process that partition's relevant sequence consistently, and use versions to reject stale updates. Different partitions do not provide a global order; partition-count and producer changes need migration planning.|key;partition;version~stale;global|More Kafka partitions preserve a single global event order automatically.|Two account balance updates arrive on different partitions and are applied out of order. Propose a correction.|Route one account to a stable partition key, carry sequence/version metadata, and make handlers reject or reconcile out-of-order updates. Choose consistency needs before parallelizing application.|kafka|ordering

saga|When is a saga appropriate, and why is compensation not the same as rollback?|A saga coordinates local transactions with durable progress and compensating actions across service boundaries. Compensation is a business operation and can fail or be only partially reversible; it is not an atomic database rollback. Use idempotent steps, retries, and reconciliation.|local transaction;compensat;idempot;reconcil~fail|A saga guarantees atomic rollback of every external side effect.|An order reserves stock and charges payment, but shipping setup fails. Outline a failure-aware saga.|Persist workflow state, issue idempotent compensation/refund actions under policy, retry recoverable failures, and reconcile unresolved outcomes. Do not assume a sent email or external transfer can be erased.|outbox,aws-idempotency|transaction
